title: Checkpoint: How Science Tests Ideas
objective: After this level you can explain how controls, blinding, randomizing and replication turn a hunch into knowledge.
summary: Semmelweis tested explanations of childbed fever by their predictions: birth position failed, handwashing succeeded. Modern trials add controls, randomizing, blinding and replication.

cards.headline: The 1800s: on one maternity ward, new mothers keep dying of fever.
cards.body: A doctor there, Ignaz Semmelweis, watched an unusually high share of new mothers die of what was called childbed fever. He had a list of possible explanations. How he sorted them is this whole chapter in one story.

cards.headline: Suspect one: the birth position
cards.body: Each explanation was a hypothesis, and each made a prediction. If giving birth lying on the back caused the fever, having women labor on their sides should lower it. Semmelweis tried it. The fever didn't fall. The prediction failed, so the evidence counted against that idea, exactly as Level 63 describes.

cards.headline: Suspect two: the doctors' hands
cards.body: Doctors often came straight from autopsies to women in labor. If their unclean hands carried the fever, thorough washing with a strong disinfectant should cut it. When Semmelweis made them wash, fever rates plummeted. The prediction could have failed, Level 62 style, and it didn't. That's strong support, though not final proof.

cards.headline: Guarding the test
cards.body: Modern tests build in more protection. In many medical trials, people are randomly assigned to a treatment group or a control group, and blinding keeps them from knowing who got which, to reduce bias. Then other researchers try to replicate the result. A finding nobody can repeat, like Abderhalden's enzymes, doesn't last.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 complete
learned: How a scientific test works: a hypothesis predicts, and a failed prediction counts against it.
Why a scientific claim must be falsifiable, and how ad hoc excuses dodge the evidence.
What a scientific theory is, and why peer review and replication check claims without proving them.
How new evidence changes science's mind, and how pseudoscience moves the goalposts instead.

questions.prompt: Which of Semmelweis's explanations did the handwashing test support?

options.label: Lying on the back during birth caused it
options.rationale: That idea failed its own test.

options.label: The fever could not be prevented
Doctors' unclean hands carried the fever
The fever came from the mothers themselves
options.rationale: The test pointed to the doctors' hands.

questions.explanation: If unclean hands carried the fever, washing should cut it. Rates plummeted, supporting that explanation.

questions.prompt: Match each test or safeguard with what came of it.

pairs.right: Keeps them from knowing who got which

questions.explanation: When women labored on their sides, the fever didn't fall. When doctors washed their hands, fever rates plummeted. In modern trials, blinding keeps people from knowing who got which.

questions.prompt: "Doctors should wash their hands before births." What kind of claim is it?

options.label: A factual claim the test proved
options.rationale: The test showed what washing does; "should" adds a standard.

options.label: A matter of personal taste
options.rationale: It appeals to a standard, not a preference.

options.label: A hypothesis to be tested
options.rationale: A hypothesis explains; this says what ought to be done.

questions.explanation: It says what ought to be done, measured against a standard, so it is a value judgment. The evidence about fever supports it but does not replace the standard.

questions.prompt: Which of these claims passes Popper's falsifiability test?

options.label: Everything happens for a reason
options.rationale: No observation could ever count against it.

options.label: Luck always evens out in the end, somehow
options.rationale: "Somehow" leaves no observation that could refute it.

options.label: This bracelet works in ways no test can detect
options.rationale: It rules out any test in advance.

options.label: This medicine lowers a fever within a day

questions.explanation: A fever that stays high after a day would count against it, so some possible observation clashes with it.

questions.prompt: What separates a scientific theory from a scientific law?

options.label: Laws have more evidence behind them
options.rationale: Theories and laws don't differ in support.

options.label: Theories are hypotheses that failed
options.rationale: A theory is a well-supported explanation.

options.label: Their breadth, not how well supported they are
A theory turns into a law once enough evidence piles up
options.rationale: Theories don't graduate into laws, however much evidence piles up.

questions.explanation: Hypotheses, theories and laws differ in breadth, not in level of support; a theory never becomes a law.
